text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mayor Provenzano, Malcolm White and city council. Thank you for the opportunity to tell my story. In 1956, the city of Sault Ste. Marie purchased a piece of property that contained a large pond located at the corner of Florin Drive and Shanna Road, now known as Snowden Park, next to the Shingwauk Indian Residential School. The city initially used this property to dump waste and garbage that was trucked from the city incinerator that was located in the Wellington Street East and Florin Drive area. In 1958, then-Councilor McIntyre voiced concerns regarding the dangers that this practice posed to the residents living in this area. As children passed through this dumping ground to walk to Animal Crate Public School and who also played in the area, there was no proper fencing around the pond and the area was home to rats because of the garbage being dumped there. He was concerned about the possible liability, excuse me, the possible liability that this posed to the city. At the time, our family lived at 212 Shanna Road across the street from the pond. On Saturday, February 27th, 1960, my two brothers, Robert and Gerald, ages eight and 10, respectively, were playing by the pond. Robert slipped down the 15, 20-foot embankment and fell into the sewage garbage-filled icy water. Gerald tried to help his brother and he fell in as well. Both called out for help and four young girls from the Shingwauk Indian Residential School heard their cries for help. One helped Robert grab a floating board while another ran to a neighboring house to get help. The fire department responded as they were able to get Robert out of the pond and were able to revive him. Unfortunately, Gerald had gone under and could not be seen. A police scuba diver had to be called in to help search for Gerald. He had a difficult time trying to locate the body, taking almost an hour and a half due to the sewage and garbage-filled water. Gerald's body was recovered just as my father, Charles, arrived at the scene. He clapped at the sight of the scuba diver holding Gerald's body over his shoulder. Gerald was pronounced dead on February 27th, 1960, on my father's birthday. Robert was never the same since the incident. He was never taken to the hospital as seen by or seen by a doctor after the incident, even though he was unconscious for some time. While the neighborhood raised $100 to help for funeral costs for Gerald, the city of Sioux State failed to reach out to our family for what happened on that day. The city eventually filled in the pond and created a park on the site. This incident was front page news and well covered by the Sioux Star at that time. This incident shattered our family. My father started to drink heavily and became very abusive to my mother and my siblings. My mother struggled to raise seven children on her own while mourning the loss of her son and dealing with my abusive father. There was not a lot of direction due to the situation and the home life for the children were terrifying as well. We were all fearful of my father. In 1978, my brother Keith died at the age of 24 when he fell from a balcony to his death. In 1979, my brother David was 21 and he burned up in a house fire. In 1980, my brother John, who was 20 years old, was crushed in a truck rollover. In 2009, my father Charles passed away at the age of 86. And in 2015, my mother Eve died, she was 88. In the 70s, we made several requests to the city to have some sort of memorial erected at Snowden Park to remember Gerald. Our requests at that time were ignored by various mayors and councilors. That's pretty well my story, but I would like to extend a sincere thank you to Ed Sadowski and Irene Barbeau for the support they have provided me. Thank you to Mayor Provenzano and Malcolm White for their understanding and for the letter of apology. On behalf of the city of Sault Ste. Marie, this is the closure for my family that I wanted and I thank you very much.

text: Again, thank you very much, Mr. Mayor, members of Council. Thank you for having me to present this. The City of Sault Ste. Marie engaged us in the fall of 2020 to look at relocating, the possibility or options of relocating the existing terminal to 111 Huron Street, or to stay and upgrade the existing terminal site. There was also two fringe options on the table with various parking alternatives on Queen Street and Bay Street, which resulted in from a previous study, which I will go forward with here shortly. Next slide, please, Ms. Zepa. First and foremost, I'd like to extend my sincere thanks to Mr. Laming and Mrs. Maione, their help and their resources in completing the study is invaluable. Specifically, their knowledge with respect to transit operations, their ridership info, was second to none, and I want to extend the thanks, and Council should be aware of their hard work and dedication to this. Next slide, please. I'm sure Council by now is all aware of the environmental assessment process, which the Engineering Department and municipalities undertake in order to plan various projects. This project is no different. It falls under what we term as a Schedule A Municipal Class Environmental Assessment. A Municipal Class Environmental Assessment is unique in a way that Schedule A and A-plus are essentially deemed by the province to be projects that have minimal environmental impact. As compared to a Schedule B or Schedule C project, which are much more in-depth and are planned accordingly, a Schedule A and A-plus are exempt projects from part two of the Environmental Assessment Act. For the information of Council, a part two is the appeal process of an environmental assessment, thus it is exempt. It's formally referred to as a pre-approved project, but the wording of that has just recently been changed to an exempt project. The implications of that is that the decision of Council tonight is final, and there is no appeal process from a member of the public to the province. The second item with respect to the Class EA process is the consultation requirements between a Schedule A, Schedule B, and Schedule C. In a Schedule B process, the minimum consultation requirements are such that advertisement of notice of public commencement to the public. There is a presentation or a public consultation with respect to the preliminary preferred alternative, where the consultant completes all their studies and selects a preliminary preferred and then goes out to the public to solicit comment, concerns, feedback, et cetera. Similarly, with the Schedule C, there's actually a second public consultation phase once the, I want to say the design, for lack of better words, is more refined. A notice of study completion is then published with the province and in local newspapers and to the public, and then the project proceeds from there provided there is no bump-up request. During the planning, the initial phases of this study and consultation with the city, it was determined that the requirements of Schedule A-plus consultation, which is limited to the city strictly notifying the public of a project. There's essentially no need for a consultation. It is, we are doing this. Credit staff, this was deemed inappropriate, and public consultation, increased public consultation with respect to this project was implemented, and we'll go through that later in the presentation. Next slide, please. The existing terminal located at the corner of Queen and Dennis was constructed in the early 80s. It's a single-story wood frame and masonry building and has an approximate area or size of 2,200 square feet. The 2018 asset management plan completed by another consultant on behalf of the city concluded that approximately $377,000 in maintenance and repairs would be required over the next five years. I'd also like to note that this report was prepared in 2018, so that five-year timeframe is, we were essentially at the twilight of that. At the time in 2018, the estimated cost to renovate the existing building was $272,000. We have adjusted that cost to attempt to reflect for 2021 pricing and for the wide variations in materials costs that we are seeing in the construction sector now due to external factors such as the pandemic. Generally speaking, the problem or the opportunity presents itself primarily for two reasons. One is the federal government and the province has come out with the ISIP, Investing in Canada Infrastructure Program, Transit Stream, and has provided the city with significant dollar amounts to allocate towards their transit system. This includes not only buses and other transportation-related upgrades, but also facilities upgrades that can be applied to. With the terminal reaching the end of its useful life, the opportunity exists to look at various alternatives. The existing terminal due to its age, congested site, its experiences, problems with the AODA compliance, accessible washrooms, accessibility, et cetera, on site, deteriorating conditions, and operational issues such as the requirement for transit operators to deadhead from there to the 111 Huron Street has led for the city to consider this relocation. I'd also like to point out that this opportunity has presented itself in numerous past reports that the city has completed. And we'll go through that here in the next slide. As the segue from the previous slide, in 2018, the city had a transit route optimization study completed by the Transit Consulting Network. In that report, various downtown terminal options were presented. As I alluded to at the start of the presentation, on-site, on-street bus parking along Queen Street, on-street bus parking along Bay Street were two options which fell off the running fairly quickly due to traffic and pedestrian safety. The two other options were provide a bus transit terminal location at the transit center. And the other option that was presented was maintained the stay and upgrade option of the existing terminal. There are also additional studies, as I alluded to in the previously, additional studies such as the 2017 Transit Relocation Feasibility Study looked at consolidating transit operations in Sackville. So moving the 111 Huron Street Maintenance Facility up to the Sackville, that was not recommended in the EA due to the operational issues that the city would continue to experience. An additional recommendation in that report was to again, review relocating the Dentistry Terminal to 111 Huron Street in order to improve operations. There's also been various council reports dating back to 2005 that has, I don't want to say recommended, but has indicated the opportunity to move the Dentistry Terminal to 111 Huron Street to recognize the operational efficiencies and increase safety, et cetera. Something that I do want to draw attention to and what occurred in 2005 as part of the GFL construction and the new arena construction is the existing terminal used to have the ability for buses to completely encircle the existing building, to pull in 360 degrees around that existing building. Due to zoning and parking requirements for the new GFL Center, that parking lot was split and thus the parking lot, which you see on the north and west sides of the building was created separate from the terminal location. That required a realignment or reorganization of the buses to the south side of the building along Queen Street. That has congested the site, that has created a number of pedestrian conflicts and it does limit the ability for the city to expand the number of buses that could be located at that site. Next slide, please. So building on the 2018 Transit Route Optimization Study, we looked at the proposed location of 111 Huron Street and went through the checklist to completing the diligence for the life cycle costs, the economics. Can the site be upgraded to the AODA compliant facilities? Are operational and safety improvements recognized at the new site? Will moving the terminal achieve these goals? Will improve the communications, management, traffic staff maintenance? And of utmost importance was, can this be done without decreasing service levels? In terms of the movement of riders, efficiency in the system, ease of use of the transit system was something that weighed heavily on our recommendations. Next slide, please. No decrease in transit service levels is a primary concern of the operation staff. What has come out of the Transit Route Optimization Study was a series of recommendations. Return of late evening Sunday service that has been successfully implemented by the city. The establishment of East-West connectors to reduce the need to travel downtown to transfer. That is ongoing. The feasibility of establishing and Central Northern Transit Mobility Hub, essentially the Northern Transfer Hub, that has been completed and is now in service. Reduce the times needed to get from point A to B, anywhere in the city to within 60 minutes, that is in progress. And the latest discussions I've had with staff that that is progressing quite well. Transit fare pricing. Use of smart car technology is in progress. Confirmation that a downtown transit terminal should be retained. There is no doubt that a downtown terminal is needed based on the spoke-style system that the current system operates at. Accelerated fleet renewal and modernization. I'm sure Mr. Laming will be happy to report to you here after me that there are 14 new buses to arrive in 2021. And embracing new technology to improve fare collection and provide real-time scheduling information on ongoing laundering is in progress. And that, I believe, is going to be incorporated with the new bus system, or the new buses coming. We do recognize that the transit cannot be all things to all people, but the Kevin Costner film, Field of Dreams, if you build it, they will come. If you make it easy for the users and efficient for users, it has been shown that you increase ridership. So that is the goal. Next slide, please. The existing terminal continues to experience deterioration. It is in need of a new roof. The HVAC system is on its last legs and is in need of some attention. The accessibility and barrier-free concerns of the current washroom setup, there's no easy way to reconfigure it. The existing washrooms just aren't large enough to meet current AODA compliance. The new, and for example, like the new turnaround for wheelchair, the full-size adult change tables that are now required for AODA compliance. These are the things that we looked at when assessing accessibility and ease of upgrading the existing building. The remaining life of the asset, per the asset management report, they have identified that this building is at or near the end of its useful life. There are inadequate facilities for security. Staff facilities, oversight, security cameras, things to improve the safety for both staff and the public. As well, deteriorating interior facilities, the exterior infrastructure is also in need of attention. New roof, we live in a very harsh climate where the asphalt and the curbs are at that point of their life where we will start seeing acceleration of deterioration. Next slide, please. Improving safety is a top priority for the city, both for their staff and for the public. The terminal has an average of 9.9 reportable incidents per month over the last three years. By reportable incidents, that does not necessarily involvement by the Sault Ste. Marie Police Services, but it is a reportable offense by security with transit. Operations are remote from other transit staff, that if there is an issue, they are further down the road, response times are lacking. If there is a maintenance issue or something like that, which I'll touch on later, that poses challenges as well. These items can be addressed by upgrading security systems within the existing terminal. However, that does not address the remoteness for other staff. Next slide, please. The Dent Street Terminal has a number of inefficiencies ceased with the current facilities. By relocating to 111 Huron Street, AODA compliance can be achieved. I'm hesitant to say it's a little bit more of a blank slate, but the renovations due to the space are easier. Bus pathways and pedestrian safety can be improved. If you recall my discussion on the Queen Street and when the buses all had to be relocated to the Queen Street side of the existing terminal, that created conflict points with pedestrians walking on the sidewalk on Queen Street, blind spots, and more unwanted interaction between pedestrians and buses. The layout that can be achieved at the 111 Huron Street addresses that, and it does make for a safer, less congested site. Staff being located at the end of points, there's no deadhead requiring. This works out to be a significant consideration from the point of air emissions and also fuel savings. Approximately $66,000 a year can be saved in fuel alone by the loss of this deadheading amount. If there is a breakdown, staff are there, and it's an easier place to switch buses out should a breakdown or a switching of buses be required due to a maintenance issue. Next slide, please. A review, the city of Saint-Marie, when we were staff and ourselves, when we were discussing service levels, a key consideration that we wanted to keep in mind was the ability for people to continue to access and get on and off at their location. There's a large number of existing stops within the downtown core. It was felt at the start, prior to optimizing any routes, that if we can maintain or expand as many existing stops and routes within the downtown core, specifically through and by the existing dentistry terminal location, then the impacts could be reduced by any sort of move. For example, and I'll use this, if a patron was traveling to the station mall, three of the seven routes currently go to the mall themselves. Under, if a proposed move to 111 Huron Street occurs, five of the seven routes will still traverse past the Queen and Dentistry intersection. So if a stop was maintained there, people would continue to get off the stop at Queen and Dennis and walk to the mall, as many still do, as evidenced by a rider survey. The two West End routes would transfer at the 111 Huron Street, and they would simply get on a bus that had a direct route to the mall.
